chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, all from Ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Raib, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

There was a slave girl for Umm Salma, the wife of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), who stole from a group of people. So she was brought to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family). Umm Salma spoke to him regarding her. The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'O Umm Salma! This is a Hadd (fixed penalty) from the Hadd of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which is not to be neglected.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) cut her.

key_terms.أُمُّ سَلَمَةَ: Umm Salma, wife of the Prophet
key_terms.حَدٌّ: Fixed penalty or legal limit prescribed by Sharia
key_terms.حُدُودِ اللَّهِ: The limits or penalties of Allah
key_terms.فَقَطَعَهَا: So he cut her (referring to the hand)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on intercession regarding the fixed penalty (Hadd) for theft in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the principle of equality in applying divine law, showing that the Prophet (peace be upon him) did not exempt Umm Salma’s slave despite her high social status, emphasizing that 'Hadd' penalties are fixed rights of God rather than discretionary favors. It serves as a foundational text in Shia jurisprudence for rejecting the notion of 'intercession' (shafa'ah) in overriding established legal penalties, reinforcing the justice and impartiality of the Prophet’s governance.
